To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) the composition of archaeal tetraether liposomes varies with pH and phylogenetic composition in geothermal springs in YNP; 2) the degree of cyclized tetraether lipid membranes is a key phenotypic trait enabling archaeal adaptation to acidity; and 3) the ability to adjust membrane composition likely represents a key factor that enabled the diversification of thermophilic archaea into environments characterized by extreme pH and temperature.
the composition of tetraether liposomes is a critical phenotypically plastic trait that enabled archaea to diversify into environments characterized by extreme pH and temperature.
the degree of cyclisation of tetraether lipds is related to the pH of the environment and this may be related to the phylogenetic relatedness of archaeal 165 rRNA gene sequences.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the relationship between archaeal lipid composition and the adaptation to extreme environments.
the role of lipid composition in the adaptation of thermophilic archaea to acidity.
the relationship between geochemistry, archaeal 16s rRNA gene diversity, and tetraether lipid membrane composition in Yellowstone hot springs.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the composition of tetraether lipides are highly variable in the geothermal springs of YNP, and the variation is best explained by variation in pH.
the ability to modify the degree of cyclisation of tetraether liposomes is an important trait for the adaptation of archaeal cells to extreme environments.

archaeal 16-S rRNA genes and GDGTs are both good indicators for the archaeal community in geothermal springs and sediments, but that they are different in their response to environmental parameters, especially pH.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the ability to alter GDGT lipid cyclization represents a critical trait that enabled the evolution of archaea in extreme environments.
the composition of tetraether liposomes is related to both the geochemistry and the phylogenetic diversity of archaeal communities in Yellowstone geothermal springs.
archaeal adaptation to low pH and high temperatures was enabled, in part, by the capacity to adjust the composition and degree of cyclization in their membranes.
The main takeaway from our work is that
archaeal lipid membranes have evolved to adjust the degree of cyclisation of tetraether lipds in order to maintain cellular homeostasis and membrane function in the face of geochemical stress.
the ability to alter the degree of cyclisation of GDGTs is a key phenotypic trait for adaptation to low pH.
the composition of GDGTs is not only a function of the phylogenetic affiliation of the producing archaeon but also a function of environmental parameters such as pH, temperature, and/or salinity.
